item.title: It wasn’t me! On white normativity and the import of RWFs — Fri Nov 6, 11:00 AM — None
item.description:
In this talk, Professor Bonilla-Silva will discuss his theoretical work on structural racism. He will review the work he has done since his 1997 article, "Rethinking Racism: Toward a Structural Interpretation," appeared in the American Sociological Review. After the review, he will address three components of his most recent theoretical work, namely, white normativity and racial habituation, racial subjectivation and RWF (regular white folks), and the significance of variance within racial groups for racial change and, unfortunately, also for maintaining racial domination. The thread that unites this talk is the idea that racial domination is not fundamentally reproduced by the actions of those traditionally viewed as "the racists" (southern, working-class, undereducated, MAGA-type Whites), but by very nice, often liberal Whites.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Mounting Tensions: Asian American Museums and the Politics of Community — Fri Nov 6, 11:00 AM — East Duke Parlors
item.description: Today, more than 40 Asian American museums operate across the United States. In the past 2 years alone, 3 such museums have opened, including the AAPI History Museum in Providence, Rhode Island; the Museum of Asian Texans in Dallas, Texas; and the Filipino American Museum in Las Vegas, Nevada. More are surely on the way as a bipartisan commission is expected to deliver its report to Congress this fall regarding the feasibility of establishing a national museum of Asian American history and culture. These institutions join older museums like the Wing Luke in Seattle and the Chinese Historical Society of America in San Francisco that date back to the civil rights struggles and immigration reforms of the 1960s. Drawing on sources and methods in U.S. cultural history, Asian American studies, and museum studies, this talk charts the changing landscape of Asian American museums and explores why and how museums have been meaningful forms of community-building and activism for Asian Americans

item.title: CCN Colloquium: "Picture That! The Mismeasure of Mental Images" — Fri Nov 6, 12:00 PM — LSRC - DIBS B035 Multipurpose Room
item.description: Mental imagery - the ability to visualize in the absence of external stimulation - plays important roles in our lives: from spatial navigation and mental rotation to reliving past events and simulating future scenarios. The subjective nature of mental imagery, however, poses serious challenges for scientists looking to understand and precisely measure this inner phenomenon. In this talk, I will share recent work from our laboratory showing different ways in which we can improve the measurement of imagery vividness, for example, by relying on physiological measures such as pupillometry. By leveraging behavioral tools from vision science, we can also better characterize visual properties of mental images, such as sharpness or saturation, and show how these relate to vividness ratings. item.title: Environmental Exposures Before Pregnancy: An Understudied Window of Vulnerability and Opportunity for Intervention — Fri Nov 6, 12:00 PM — None
item.description:
Developmental toxicology often focuses on exposures during pregnancy, but a mother's health before conception may also shape the conditions in which pregnancy begins. This seminar examines that possibility through a mouse study of preconception exposure to a mixture of phthalates at a human-relevant dose, with exposure ending before mating. Findings span the maternal, fetal, and adult offspring health outcomes, including changes in placental structure, sex-specific placental gene expression, altered growth trajectories, and changes in metabolic programming. These results raise questions about how preconception exposures may influence pregnancy and development, which biological pathways may be involved, and how future research could identify opportunities for prevention before pregnancy.
This seminar will be held in Grainger Hall room 1112 and online via Panopto. Click "More Event Information" to visit the seminar website for a link to attend virtually. Both attendance options are free

Duke University Libraries will be turning the pages of the Birds of America on the first Friday of every month! We welcome you to stop by and watch-what bird will be next?
Birds of America is one of the greatest undertakings in the history of both art and ornithology. Almost 200 years after its publication, it remains a primary resource for scientists and scholars. This four-volume, double-elephant-folio edition on handmade paper measures three feet tall and two feet wide and comprises 435 hand-colored prints impressed from copperplate engravings. Of the original 175 to 200 complete sets, 125 have survived. Nine species of those depicted have since gone extinct.

item.title: The Comeback of Blue-Throated Macaws — Sat Nov 14, 1:00 PM — Nature Research Center
item.description:
20 years of conservation success: the comeback of blue-throated macaws
Join us along with the Wake Audubon Society in the SECU Daily Planet Theater for a special presentation with Dorothy Paterson, executive director for Bird Endowment. Ms. Dorothy Paterson, the President & Executive Director of Bird Endowment, will join us via Zoom to deliver “Twenty Years of Conservation Success: The Comeback of Blue-Throated Macaws” inside the SECU Daily Planet Theater. Blue-Throated Macaws are a critically endangered parrot native exclusively to the Beni Savannas of north-central Bolivia. Only 300-500 individuals remain in the wild. Their severe decline is driven by habitat loss, the illegal pet trade, and the historic use of its feathers in traditional dances.
Source: NC Museum of Natural Sciences

item.title: From Pizza to Plant Leaves: The Mathematics of Thin Materials | Carolina Science Café — Tue Dec 1, 6:00 PM — Haw River Tap & Table
item.description:
Why do plant leaves curl as they grow or dry out? Why do you fold a slice of pizza when picking it up? How can inflatable structures support heavy loads? At December’s Carolina Science Café, Dr. Thomas Chandler will explore these questions through the lens of applied mathematics. He will introduce the mechanics of thin elastic materials, showing how geometry and the competition between bending and stretching govern their behavior. From Gauss’s remarkable theorem to the design of soft robots, he will demonstrate how these mathematical ideas help us understand biological structures and inspire new technologies.

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Thu Feb 4 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.title: Understanding Obesity: From Stigma to Surgery — Fri Nov 6 — None
item.description:
The United States population increasingly meets the criteria for obesity. In recent years, new options for treatment have developed, and more patients are seeking support from their healthcare providers. As a result, front-line providers are tasked more frequently with assessing treatment options and managing patients with obesity. Multidisciplinary treatment requires cooperation and integration of all relevant disciplines and specialties, which are critical to provide excellent patient care, improve the patient experience, and achieve better outcomes. Understanding Obesity: From Stigma to Surgery will provide valuable information on available treatment options, including diet, psychology, medication, and surgical options. Attendees will gain an understanding of empathetic and non-judgmental approaches to patient care and will learn the impact of the interrelationship between obesity and associated health issues.
